title: Current financial confidence is age-stratified while future security remains broadly uncertain across generations
source_unit: Edward Jones-Gallup, Money and Meaning: Understanding Financial Fulfillment, September 15, 2026
geography: United States and Canada; adults aged 21 and older, with generation and life-stage comparisons

observations.period: March-April 2026 survey; confidence managing current versus future finances

denominator.unit: more than 5,000 U.S. adults surveyed; study also interviewed more than 2,000 Canadian adults

us_current_gen_z.unit: percent of U.S. Gen Z adults expressing a great deal of confidence managing current financial needs

us_current_gen_x.unit: percent of U.S. Gen X adults

us_current_age_range.unit: percentage-point range between U.S. baby boomers and Gen Z on current-finance confidence

observations.method: Edward Jones-Gallup Money and Meaning study interviewing more than 5,000 U.S. adults and more than 2,000 Canadian adults aged 21 and older in March and April 2026; public summary reports generation comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The public article provides lower-bound total sample descriptions rather than exact analytic denominators and does not establish whether age differences reflect wealth, income, life stage, cohort, health, housing or survey interpretation.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Gen Z adults aged 21-29, millennials aged 30-46, Gen X aged 47-61 and baby boomers aged 62-80.
observations.counterinterpretation: Older adults may report greater current confidence because they have more accumulated assets and fewer acquisition goals, not because they face fewer financial risks overall.

observations.period: March-April 2026 survey; future-finance confidence converges across generations

denominator.unit: more than 5,000 U.S. adults surveyed; exact generation-specific denominators not disclosed in the public summary

us_future_gen_z.unit: percent of U.S. Gen Z adults expressing a great deal of confidence managing future financial needs

us_future_gen_x.unit: percent of U.S. Gen X adults

future_current_convergence.value: Future-finance confidence differs less by generation than current-finance confidence, and even Gen X remains below one-third expressing a great deal of confidence.

observations.method: Generation comparison of confidence in managing future financial needs in the Edward Jones-Gallup study.
observations.uncertainty: Confidence is a subjective expectation and not a projection of retirement adequacy, savings balances, debt, income replacement or future consumption; the study is not a longitudinal wealth panel.
observations.subgroup: U.S. generations, with parallel Canada comparisons in the source.
observations.counterinterpretation: Future uncertainty may reflect different financial goals and time horizons across life stages rather than a shared deterioration in expected security.

observations.period: March-April 2026 survey; Gen X retirement planning and perceived control

denominator.unit: U.S. Gen X subgroup; public article does not disclose subgroup count

gen_x_has_retirement_plan.unit: percent of U.S. Gen X adults reporting a retirement financial plan

gen_x_savings_may_not_last.unit: percent of U.S. Gen X adults worried current and future savings will not last

gen_x_control_with_plan.unit: percent of U.S. Gen X adults with a retirement plan reporting a great deal of control over their financial future

gen_x_control_without_plan.value: About one-fifth of Gen X adults overall report a great deal of control; worry about savings is 59% among those without a plan versus 25% among those with a plan.

observations.method: Descriptive comparison of Gen X retirement planning, savings-duration worry and perceived control.
observations.uncertainty: Planning is associated with confidence and lower worry but the cross-sectional data do not show that planning causes control, adequacy or realized retirement security; financial capacity may enable both.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Gen X adults aged 47-61, by reported retirement-plan status.
observations.counterinterpretation: A plan may be a marker of higher income, financial literacy, employer access or accumulated assets rather than an independent protection.

observations.period: March-April 2026 survey; younger-adult financial stress, extra work and life tradeoffs

denominator.unit: U.S. generation subgroups; public article does not disclose subgroup counts

gen_z_financial_stress.unit: percent of U.S. Gen Z adults always or often experiencing financial stress

gen_x_financial_stress.unit: percent of U.S. Gen X adults

gen_z_working_more_than_wanted.unit: percent of employed U.S. Gen Z adults working more hours than desired to increase income

gen_x_working_more_than_wanted.unit: percent of employed U.S. Gen X adults

gen_z_finances_control_life.unit: percent of U.S. Gen Z adults saying finances always or often control their lives

life_stage_room_mechanism.value: Younger adults are converting financial pressure into extra work, delayed asset-building and sacrificed priorities while trying to build income and wealth.

observations.method: Descriptive generation comparisons of financial stress, work hours, sacrificed priorities and perceived financial control.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are self-reported and cross-sectional; they do not quantify hours, income, asset accumulation, causal tradeoffs or future financial outcomes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Gen Z, millennials, Gen X and baby boomers, with Canada comparisons in the source.
observations.counterinterpretation: Generational differences may partly reflect age, employment stage, household composition and different definitions of financial goals rather than a single cohort condition.

boundary: This record adds a life-course household-security mechanism: current financial confidence is strongly age-stratified, while confidence in the future remains comparatively low across generations; younger adults absorb pressure through stress, extra work and delayed wealth-building, and Gen X faces a retirement-control gap. The study does not establish causal cohort effects, financial adequacy, realized retirement outcomes, asset distributions or policy impact.
